pages.headline: Deliver more projects without betting the firm on the hiring market.
pages.outcome: Your growth plan has one engine: hire senior engineers and architects fast enough to keep up with the work you win. The market takes years to make one and your competitors are bidding for the same people. Governed AI adds a second engine. Drafting, retrieval, and assembly move onto rails, senior technical attention returns to scoping, estimating, and standing behind what ships, and revenue can move faster than headcount without the firm's delivery reputation paying for it.
triggers: The growth plan assumes senior engineers and architects the market will not supply at a price your rates can carry.

Two fixed bids in a row overran, and nobody can say from the data which part of the estimate was wrong.
Clients have started asking how the firm uses AI inside their environments, and the answer depends on which engineer they ask.

evidence.text: In a field experiment with 758 consultants at one elite firm, AI use on tasks inside its capability frontier meant 12.2 percent more tasks completed, 25.1 percent faster, at more than 40 percent higher judged quality than the control group.
evidence.caveat: Task-level results at one elite global firm on consulting-style knowledge tasks, the closest causal analog to this work and still not engineering delivery or mid-market proof. The same study found quality fell when AI was used outside the frontier, which is what the review gates are for. No public causal study measures AI's return for a mid-market IT consulting firm.

evidence.text: In a preregistered experiment with roughly 453 college-educated professionals, access to a general AI assistant cut time on mid-level professional writing tasks by about 40 percent and raised evaluator-scored quality by about 18 percent.
evidence.caveat: Controlled, occupation-specific writing tasks, not client engagements, engineering work, or estimates. What AI assistance does to estimate accuracy has not been measured anywhere public.

pages.headline: One governed platform, instead of an assistant in every project team.
pages.outcome: The firm is already using AI, approved or not, and some of it is running inside client environments. The question on your desk is whether that becomes a platform you can operate and defend or a sprawl you get blamed for. A second question belongs to you alone: a firm that implements AI for clients cannot be found running it ungoverned at home. Governed AI operations gives you the architecture: project-scoped access, approved tools and sources, provenance by default, and a sanctioned path fast enough that engineers stop wanting the other one.

pages.headline: An AI posture you could walk a client's security team through.
pages.outcome: The risk is not that the firm uses AI. It is that the firm cannot say where, under whose account, inside which client environment, and under what controls. Your exposure is unusual: the firm works inside other organizations' systems, holds their credentials, and may serve their competitors. Governed AI operations replaces improvisation with a defensible posture: client and contract boundaries, credentials out of prompts, provenance on generated code, an accountable engineer at every gate, and evidence that reconstructs what happened.
triggers: Client master agreements and security addenda have started speaking to AI directly, and they do not all say the same thing.

Generated code has shipped into a client's production environment with no provenance record and no license posture behind it.
A client's security team, an insurer, or an acquirer asked about AI controls, and the answer was assembled overnight.

pages.headline: An AI investment case that would survive your own estimation review.
pages.outcome: You have seen the vendor math: day-one payback, hours saved that nobody redeployed, benefits counted three times. The governed version is different by construction: baselines before pilots, program cost counted once, adoption lag priced in, ranges instead of points, and freed capacity named to a destination so it lands in margin instead of on the bench. In this business the case lives or dies on two numbers, estimate-to-actual variance and bench time, and both of them are yours to measure.

evidence.text: The most recent professional-services benchmark put surveyed billable utilization at 66.4 percent, the lowest in that survey's history and below its 75 percent target, with EBITDA around 9.9 percent.
evidence.source: SPI Research, summarized by Deltek (2025 performance); sponsored benchmark
evidence.caveat: A vendor-sponsored voluntary survey across professional-services verticals, not a census, and its IT-consulting split is not public. Utilization and EBITDA definitions vary between firms, and none of this is caused by AI. There is no public causal study of AI's return for a mid-market IT consulting firm, and the effect of AI assistance on estimate accuracy is unmeasured, which is why the baseline is the evidence.
